title: Does OSHA require workplace violence training for healthcare and social service workers?
description: OSHA's 2016 workplace violence guidelines for healthcare and social service: voluntary, no federal standard, annual training advice, stalled rulemaking.
shortAnswer: No federal OSHA standard requires workplace violence training. OSHA's Guidelines for Preventing Workplace Violence for Healthcare and Social Service Workers (OSHA 3148, 2016) are advisory and create no new legal obligations. They recommend orientation before duties, annual training for all workers and more frequent refreshers in high-risk settings. OSHA can still cite employers under the General Duty Clause, and as at November 2026 its proposed healthcare standard is a long-term action with no proposal date.
keyTakeaways: OSHA states that there are currently no specific OSHA standards for workplace violence; the 2016 guidelines are advisory and neither create nor alter legal obligations.
Employers still have the General Duty Clause, section 5(a)(1) of the Occupational Safety and Health Act, which OSHA has used in healthcare workplace violence enforcement cases.

The guidelines recommend initial orientation for new and reassigned workers, annual training for all workers, and refresher training possibly monthly or quarterly in high-risk settings, using role-play, simulations and drills.

Training is one of five building blocks of a written prevention program, alongside management commitment and worker participation, worksite analysis, hazard prevention and control, and recordkeeping and program evaluation.

OSHA's rulemaking (RIN 1218-AD08) completed a small business review in May 2023 and was listed for a June 2025 proposal in Fall 2024, but has since moved to Long-Term Actions with the proposal date to be determined.
regulator: Occupational Safety and Health Administration (OSHA), US Department of Labor
appliesTo: Hospital settings and residential treatment settings such as nursing homes and other long-term care facilities
Non-residential treatment and service settings such as neighborhood clinics and mental health centers
Community care settings such as community-based residential facilities and group homes
Field work, including home healthcare workers and social workers who make home visits
Supervisors, managers, security personnel and contract or visiting staff in these settings

sections.heading: Is there a federal OSHA standard for workplace violence in healthcare?

blocks.text: No. OSHA's [workplace violence page](https://www.osha.gov/workplace-violence) states that "there are currently no specific OSHA standards for workplace violence." The healthcare guidance itself, [OSHA 3148](https://www.osha.gov/sites/default/files/publications/osha3148.pdf), says it is advisory and informational, is not a standard or regulation, and neither creates new legal obligations nor alters existing ones.

That does not leave employers without duties. Under the [General Duty Clause](https://www.law.cornell.edu/uscode/text/29/654), section 5(a)(1) of the Occupational Safety and Health Act, each employer must furnish employment and a place of employment free from recognized hazards that are causing or likely to cause death or serious physical harm. OSHA's regulatory agenda notes that it has used the General Duty Clause in enforcement cases addressing workplace violence in healthcare. Some states with OSHA-approved state plans have their own rules; California is covered on the [California workplace violence prevention page](/regulations/california-workplace-violence-prevention-training).

sections.heading: What are OSHA's healthcare workplace violence guidelines?

blocks.text: They are OSHA publication 3148, Guidelines for Preventing Workplace Violence for Healthcare and Social Service Workers, revised in 2016. OSHA first issued them in 1996 and updated them in 2004 and 2016. They set out how to build a written violence prevention program, incorporated into the organization's overall safety and health program.

The guidelines explain why healthcare is singled out. Citing Bureau of Labor Statistics data, they report that between 2011 and 2013 workplace assaults ranged from 23,540 to 25,630 a year, with 70 to 74 percent occurring in healthcare and social service settings, and that assaults made up 10 to 11 percent of healthcare workers' injuries involving days away from work, compared with 3 percent for all private sector employees.

sections.heading: What training do the OSHA guidelines recommend?

blocks.text: Initial orientation before duties, annual training for everyone, and more frequent refreshers where risk is high. The guidelines say the training program should involve all workers, including contract workers, supervisors and managers, and that worker safety should be a separate, thoroughly addressed component even when training is combined with patient protection topics such as de-escalation.

items: New and reassigned workers should receive an initial orientation before being assigned their job duties.
All workers should receive required training annually. In high-risk settings and institutions, refresher training may be needed more frequently, perhaps monthly or quarterly.
Visiting staff, such as physicians, should receive the same training as permanent staff and contract workers.
Qualified trainers should teach at a comprehension level appropriate for the staff, and effective programs should involve role-playing, simulations and drills.
De-escalation and self-defense training should both include a hands-on component.
Every worker should understand "universal precautions for violence": violence should be expected but can be avoided or mitigated through preparation.

blocks.text: Suggested topics include the prevention policy, risk factors, documenting changes in patient or client behavior, alarm systems and safety devices, early recognition of escalating behavior, dealing with hostile relatives and visitors, safe rooms, a standard response action plan, restraint use, the buddy system, reporting and recordkeeping, and how to obtain medical care, trauma-informed care, counseling and workers' compensation after an incident.

sections.heading: What about supervisors, security staff and evaluating training?

blocks.text: The guidelines give each group its own content. Supervisors and managers should be trained to recognize high-risk situations so workers are not placed in assignments that compromise their safety, to encourage incident reporting and care after an incident, and to change the physical plant, treatment program, staffing and procedures to reduce hazards. Security personnel need site-specific training, including the psychological components of handling aggressive and abusive clients.

Training should itself be evaluated. At least annually, the team or coordinator responsible for the program should review training content, methods and frequency, using supervisor and employee interviews, testing, observation and incident reports. See [how to measure training effectiveness](/guides/how-to-measure-training-effectiveness) for evaluation methods.

The guidelines also stress anti-retaliation. Section 11(c) of the OSH Act prohibits discrimination against an employee for reporting an incident or injury related to workplace violence, and 29 CFR 1904.36 applies the same protection to reporting work-related injuries and illnesses.

sections.heading: What is the status of OSHA's healthcare workplace violence rulemaking?

blocks.text: Stalled at the pre-proposal stage as at November 2026. The Unified Agenda entry for [RIN 1218-AD08, Workplace Violence in Health Care and Social Assistance](https://www.reginfo.gov/public/do/eAgendaViewRule?pubId=202510&RIN=1218-AD08), records this timeline:

head: Date
Step
rows: Request for Information published (81 FR 88147); comment period ended April 6, 2017
OSHA granted petitions from a coalition of labor unions and from National Nurses United seeking a standard
Small Business Regulatory Enforcement Fairness Act (SBREFA) process initiated
Small Business Advocacy Review panel convened
Proposed Rule Stage, with an NPRM projected for June 2025
Moved to Long-Term Actions; NPRM date To Be Determined

blocks.text: The [Fall 2024 agenda entry](https://www.reginfo.gov/public/do/eAgendaViewRule?pubId=202410&RIN=1218-AD08) shows the earlier projection. No proposed rule has been published, so there is no proposed regulatory text to train against. Organizations should treat the guidelines as the federal benchmark and follow any state rule that applies. For tracking changes like this, see [how to update training when regulations change](/guides/how-to-update-training-when-regulations-change).

sections.heading: How can a healthcare employer map the guidelines to evidence?

blocks.text: Because the guidelines are voluntary, the practical question is what evidence would show a recognized hazard was being addressed if OSHA inspected under the General Duty Clause. The table below is an illustrative register that maps the guideline recommendations to roles, frequencies and records.

head: Recommendation
Role
Frequency
Evidence an inspector might ask for
rows: Initial orientation on hazards and procedures
New and reassigned workers, including contract staff
Orientation records with unit-specific hazard content
Workplace violence training with hands-on de-escalation
Attendance and practical assessment records from role-play or drills
Refresher logs linked to the worksite hazard analysis
Training records; incident reviews showing follow-up
Review notes covering content, methods and frequency

sections.heading: How does Knowledge Foundry approach this?

blocks.text: Knowledge Foundry maps each OSHA 3148 recommendation to learning outcomes and assessment points, such as observed de-escalation in a simulation, and tags it as guidance rather than law, so an organization can show what it adopted and why. If OSHA publishes a proposed standard, the framework can be compared against the new text clause by clause. See [healthcare and life sciences](/industries/healthcare-life-sciences).

faqs.q: Can OSHA cite a hospital for workplace violence without a specific standard?
faqs.a: Yes, under the General Duty Clause in section 5(a)(1) of the Occupational Safety and Health Act, which requires a workplace free from recognized hazards likely to cause death or serious physical harm. OSHA's regulatory agenda states it has used the clause in healthcare workplace violence enforcement cases.

faqs.q: How often does OSHA recommend workplace violence training in healthcare?
faqs.a: The 2016 guidelines recommend initial orientation for new and reassigned workers before they start duties and annual training for all workers. In high-risk settings and institutions, they suggest refresher training may be needed more frequently, perhaps monthly or quarterly.

faqs.q: When will OSHA publish a workplace violence standard for healthcare?
faqs.a: No date is set. The Unified Agenda lists RIN 1218-AD08 as a Long-Term Action with the proposed rule date To Be Determined, after the Fall 2024 agenda had projected a June 2025 proposal. As at November 2026 no proposed rule has been published.

faqs.q: Do the OSHA guidelines apply to home health and social workers?
faqs.a: Yes. The guidelines define five settings, including field work by home healthcare workers and social workers who make home visits, and community care settings such as group homes. Because they are advisory, they recommend practices rather than impose obligations on those employers.
